inclusionReview.note: The Cornwall–Pinguin encounter on 8 May 1941 is individually included as a naval engagement. The Australian War Memorial identifies the ships and date; the contemporary British intelligence report describes the gunnery action and sinking. This admits no other naval-warfare class instance. The inherited Wikidata event point [57.8, 3.5] remains a source locator, not an independently surveyed or newly corrected position.

note:
The comparison covers the two surface ships engaged on 8 May 1941. Cornwall survived with damage; Pinguin sank. Zero British ship loss does not mean zero damage or human casualties. Cornwall’s reconnaissance aircraft assisted the search but are not converted to ships or added to this denominator. The intelligence report is based partly on prisoner accounts and warns that details were not all verified; its conflicting casualty, prisoner and tactical claims are not adopted. No crew-death count is inferred from the sinking. Cornwall now has a separately reviewed representative County/Kent heavy-cruiser profile for 1941. Pinguin’s armed-merchant-raider equipment remains unreviewed; its date-based ship silhouette is generic.

Cornwall is illustrated by an original County/Kent heavy-cruiser family model based on its as-fitted December 1937 refit plan and 1938 broadside photograph. Three raked funnels, four twin main turrets in fore-and-aft superfiring pairs, and aircraft-handling structures distinguish it from a generic industrial warship. This is a post-refit silhouette analogy for the reviewed 1941 action, not an exact reconstruction of its radar, light anti-aircraft weapons, camouflage or every deck fitting. No aircraft are added to the ship cohort. Pinguin and every strength, loss and death field are unchanged. The Cornwall–Pinguin encounter on 8 May 1941 is individually included as a naval engagement.
